Learning Objectives
Detail the anatomy of the brachial plexus.
Describe the anatomy of the shoulder girdle pertaining to brachial plexus injuries.
Review of different types of brachial plexus injuries, clinical manifestations, and treatment
options.
Explain the goals of shoulder reconstruction in patients with a traumatic brachial plexus injury.
Review the treatment options available for shoulder reconstruction in patients with a
traumatic brachial plexus injury.

Overview
Brachial plexus injuries (BPIs) are devastating injuries that predominantly affect young, healthy
individuals.
They may involve all the roots (pan-plexus), presenting as a flail arm, or upper plexus palsy
(C5-6 ± C7), presenting as denervation of the biceps, brachialis, deltoid, and rotator cuff
muscles.
In these patients, restoration of elbow flexion is the highest priority, followed by restoration of
glenohumeral abduction, shoulder stability, and external rotation.
Epidemiology
Most commonly occurs in young males aged 15 to 30 years.1
70% of injuries are supraclavicular, meaning that injury is to the nerve roots or trunks.
Complete pan-plexus injuries, which involve all the roots (C5 through T1), are the most
common type, with widely varying degrees of recovery.
75% to 80% of traumatic BPIs
Upper trunk injuries (C5-C6) compose 20% to 25% of traumatic BPIs and typically result from
high-energy trauma that forces the shoulder in a caudal direction.
Lower trunk injuries (C7 through T1) account for 0.6% to 3.0% of traumatic BPIs and may
result from forced shoulder abduction.1
Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus and Shoulder Girdle
Neural Anatomy
Composition
The brachial plexus is an arrangement of nerve fibers formed by the ventral rami of the C5
through T1 nerve roots, with rare contributions from the C4 spinal nerves (prefixed plexus;
Figure 1) and the T2 spinal nerves (postfixed plexus; Figure 2).

The brachial plexus is divided into five anatomic sections (Figure 3): the spinal nerves; the
superior, middle, and inferior trunks; the retroclavicular divisions; the medial, lateral, and
posterior cords; and the terminal branches.

Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Spinal nerve roots
The spinal nerve roots are formed from nerve rootlets that exit the spinal cord.
The dorsal root is the afferent sensory root. At the distal end of a dorsal root is a coalescence
of nerve cell bodies called the dorsal root ganglion, which conveys sensory input back to the
spinal cord (Figure 4).
The ventral root (motor) joins the dorsal root distal to the dorsal root ganglion and forms the
spinal nerve. The cell bodies of the ventral root lie within the anterior horn of the spinal cord
gray matter.

Figure 4 Illustration shows the anatomy of the brachial plexus roots (A) and the common
types of injury: avulsion (B), stretch (C), and rupture (D). Traction to the brachial plexus may
cause nerve injuries of varying severity. Avulsion (preganglionic) injuries of the nerve roots
from the spinal cord cannot, for practical purposes, be repaired. With stretch (postganglionic)
injuries, some spontaneous recovery is possible. Extraforaminal rupture of the nerve or
trunk can be repaired surgically. (Reproduced with permission from the Mayo Foundation for
Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Injury location
Lesions that occur proximal to the dorsal root ganglion are called preganglionic or
supraganglionic.
Lesions distal to the dorsal root ganglion are called postganglionic or infraganglionic.
Anatomy pearls
Terminal nerve branches that arise from the root level are clinically important because they
may indicate the level of the lesion.

These include the phrenic nerve (arising from C3 through C5), the dorsal scapular nerve to
the rhomboid muscles (arising from C5), and the long thoracic nerve to the serratus anterior
muscle (arising from C5 through C7).
If these muscles function and paralysis of the arm is present distally, the injury to the
brachial plexus must have occurred distal to their takeoff of the associated nerve root (ie,
postganglionic).
The only terminal nerve branch off the trunk level is the suprascapular nerve (innervating the
infraspinatus and supraspinatus), which branches off the upper trunk at the Erb point. No
terminal branches off the division level exist.
Biomechanics of Shoulder Girdle
The glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, and sternoclavicular joints and the scapulothoracic
articulation create three-dimensional shoulder motion controlled by 14 muscles.
Eight muscles move the glenohumeral joint: latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, deltoid,
supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis, teres minor, and teres major.
Six muscles support the scapula on the chest wall: serratus anterior, trapezius, rhomboid
minor, rhomboid major, levator scapulae, and pectoralis minor.
Reconstruction of prime movers/stabilizers of the glenohumeral joint is prioritized, followed by
scapular stabilizers/movers in BPIs

Biomechanics of Shoulder Girdle
Knowledge of shoulder anatomy and biomechanics is critical to apprehend shoulder
reconstruction in BPIs. Goldner2 divided the muscles about the shoulder into four
functional groups: group 1, the prime movers, includes the clavicular head of the
pectoralis major and deltoid; group 2, the stabilizers, includes the subscapularis,
supraspinatus, and infraspinatus; group 3, the depressors, includes the teres major,
biceps, latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, and triceps; and group 4, the accessory
stabilizers of the scapula, includes the trapezius, serratus anterior, pectoralis minor,
levator scapulae, and rhomboids. Rotator cuff muscles are the primary stabilizers of the
glenohumeral joint during shoulder motion. The stabilizing effect of the rotator cuff
muscles (via a force couple created by the subscapularis anteriorly and the infraspinatus
posteriorly) resists a relative upward shearing moment at the glenohumeral joint created

by the contracting deltoid muscle during early abduction. Effective function of the
deltoid (prime mover of the shoulder) is substantially compromised if the stabilizing
function of the rotator cuff is lost or deficient. The accessory stabilizers of the scapula
are an important group of muscles that stabilize and mobilize the scapula on the chest
wall and are essential to complement shoulder motion in abduction and flexion. Better
shoulder functional outcomes have been reported in patients with BPI who had partial
or full recovery or preservation of the serratus anterior than in those without serratus
function.3 Therefore, if tendon transfers about the shoulder are planned, the first
priority is given to reconstruction of the prime movers and stabilizers, followed by the
scapular stabilizers/movers. In most adults with a BPI, reconstruction of active scapular
stabilization via tendon transfer rarely is possible because of the scarcity of available
adequately functioning muscles.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
A history of the etiology of the BPI helps determine the severity of the BPI and plan
management. Traumatic injuries typically result from high-energy accidents. An observed
worldwide increase in BPIs is thought to be the result of the increased popularity of high-
energy sports activities and increased survivorship after motor vehicle collisions secondary to
safety mechanisms (ie, airbags).
Motor vehicle collisions are the leading cause of traumatic BPIs worldwide. The approximate
rule of seven seventies may be a helpful mnemonic for remembering the etiology and location
of injuries:
70% of BPIs result from motor vehicle collisions, of which
70% involve bicycles or motorcycles
70% of patients sustain multiple injuries.
70% of BPIs are supraclavicular.
At least 70% of patients with a supraclavicular injury have at least one nerve root avulsion.
70% of these injuries involve a lower root (C7, C8, T1).
Chronic pain develops in 70% of these patients.
Direction of force on the upper extremity
Trauma that forces the arm/shoulder caudally (eg, fall onto the shoulder) may result in
injuries that predominantly affect the upper portions of the brachial plexus; however, with
enough energy, these injuries can disrupt all roots of the plexus (Figure 5).

Figure 5 Illustrations show an injury that predominantly affects the upper portions of the
brachial plexus. Injury patterns often may be predicted. A, Injuries to the upper brachial
plexus occur if the shoulder is forced downward and the head is forced to the opposite side.
This injury pattern often is referred to as an Erb-Duchenne palsy. B, The direction of force, as
shown by the curved arrow, may cause the C5 through T1 nerve roots to be avulsed or
ruptured as shown. (Reproduced with permission from the Mayo Foundation for Medical
Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Trauma that forces the arm/shoulder into violent abduction (eg, restraining a fall, having the
arm pulled away) may result in injury to the lower plexus elements, with a variable degree of
injury to the upper elements (Figure 6).
Gunshot wounds also may result in BPI, with the severity depending on the caliber, velocity,
and angle of entry of the missile. High-velocity missiles typically cause nerve injury via
shockwave and cavitation effects, which cause nerve contusion and traction rather than
direct nerve impact.

Associated Injuries
Polytrauma/multisystem injuries
Shoulder fracture-dislocation; clavicle, scapular, rib, and cervical fractures
Vascular injuries
Classification of BPIs
Preganglionic versus postganglionic
Preganglionic BPIs, often referred to as root avulsions, are not repairable because the
rootlets are avulsed from the spinal cord. They are called preganglionic because the injury
has occurred proximal to the dorsal root ganglion.
Postganglionic BPIs occur distal to the dorsal root ganglion and can be repaired by restoring
nerve continuity, depending on the mechanism and location of the injury. Mechanisms of
injury include lacerations, penetrating injuries, or traction (that results in rupture or stretch
injuries)

Level of injury—Multiple classification schemes for BPIs have been described. The most
descriptive system classifies BPIs according to the anatomic level of injury.
Injuries often are multilevel, occurring between the two points such that the nerve is fixed,
restrained by surrounding structures, or changes in direction.
General description: supraclavicular, retroclavicular, or infraclavicular
The reported injury frequencies by level are shown in Table 1.

Supraclavicular injuries
C5 and C6 or upper trunk (Erb palsy) lesions account for approximately 20% to 25% of
traumatic BPIs.
C8, T1, or lower trunk (Klumpke palsy) lesions are extremely rare and account for
approximately 0.6% to 3.0% of traumatic BPIs.
The most common pattern of supraclavicular injuries is complete involvement of all roots,
which accounts for 75% to 80% of traumatic BPIs.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination

The quality of a patient’s upper extremity pain should be closely evaluated. Preganglionic
lesions often cause more severe, unbearable pain, dysesthesia, and paresthesia than
postganglionic lesions. This is secondary to the associated spinal cord injury in which the
rootlets were avulsed from the spinal cord.
All motor groups and sensory distributions innervated by the terminal branches of the plexus
should be serially examined and systematically documented (Figure 7).
This information is important for determining spontaneous recovery and for later planning of
appropriate management, including available donors for nerve or tendon transfers.
Muscle strength
Every muscle of the upper extremity should be examined, with strength graded on a five-
point scale as described by the British Medical Research Council.
Although many variations and interpretations of the British Medical Research Council grading
system exist, surgeons must be consistent with measurements and variations.
Key muscles to assess are the rhomboids and the serratus anterior.
These muscles require special attention during the physical examination because injury to
their innervating nerves (the dorsal scapular nerve for the rhomboid muscles and the long
thoracic nerve for the serratus anterior muscle) indicates a supraclavicular and possibly even
a preganglionic location of injury.
If these muscles are functional in a patient with an upper plexus palsy, the lesion most likely
is postganglionic.

Neurovascular Examination
Examination of the ipsilateral eye and eyelid
If T1 is avulsed (preganglionic injury), the sympathetic chain associated with the eye often is
injured, resulting in eyelid ptosis, meiosis (smaller pupil), and ipsilateral skin anhidrosis
(Figure 8).
This is called Horner syndrome and is pathognomonic for a preganglionic T1 avulsion.
Radial, ulnar, and brachial pulses—Evaluation of the radial, ulnar, and brachial pulses is
important because arterial injuries are very common in patients with a complete BPI. Arterial
injuries also may result in a pseudoaneurysm, which may cause a pulsatile mass or thrill on
examination.
Figure 8 Photograph demonstrates the ptosis, miosis, facial anhidrosis, and enophthalmos in
a patient with Horner syndrome resulting from a sympathetic chain palsy, which is associated
with an avulsion of the C8 and T1 nerve roots. (Reproduced with permission from the Mayo
Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)

Neurovascular Examination
A thorough examination is critical to understand the level and extent of BPI and the
availability of donors for nerve/tendon transfers for reconstructive purposes.
Preganglionic injuries imply root avulsions from the spinal cord; therefore, in these
patients, nerve repair or nerve grafting is not feasible. Evidence of paraspinal muscle
injury, rhomboid paralysis, scapular winging, Horner syndrome, hemidiaphragm
paralysis on a chest radiograph, or pseudomeningocele on a CT myelogram are
indicative of preganglionic injury. Common patterns of BPIs include the following:

Upper Trunk (C5-6 ± C7)
These patients have deficits of shoulder motor function (deltoid, rotator cuff
musculature), elbow flexion (biceps brachii, brachialis, brachioradialis), and forearm
supination (biceps brachii, supinator). Patients have normal elbow extension and normal
wrist and hand function. In many patients variable involvement of the C7 nerve root is
observed. These patients have additional deficits in elbow extension, wrist extension,
and variably digital extension and flexion.
Lower Trunk (C8, T1)
These patients have a normal functional shoulder and elbow, and deficits mainly are
limited to hand function.
Pan-plexus Injury
These patients present with a flail extremity and disability of shoulder, elbow, and hand
function.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard radiographs should include views of the cervical spine, shoulder (AP and axillary
views), and chest to identify associated injuries.
Cervical spine radiographs should be examined for any cervical fractures that may put the
spinal cord at risk.
Transverse process fractures of the cervical vertebrae may indicate root avulsion at the same
level.
A chest radiograph may demonstrate a clavicle or rib fracture (first or second ribs), suggesting
damage to the adjacent brachial plexus.
Careful review of chest radiographs may provide information regarding old rib fractures, which
may become important if intercostal nerves are considered for nerve transfers. Rib fractures
often injure the associated intercostal nerves.
If the phrenic nerve is injured, associated paralysis of the hemidiaphragm will be present. A
high probability of C5 root avulsion exists if diaphragmatic paralysis is present.

Computed Tomography
CT myelography currently is the preferred imaging modality for defining the level of nerve root
injury.
If a cervical root avulsion is present, the dural sheath heals with the development of a
pseudomeningocele.
Immediately postinjury, a blood clot often is observed in the area of the nerve root avulsion
and may displace dye from the myelogram. Therefore, CT myelography should be performed 3
to 4 weeks postinjury to allow time for any blood clots to dissipate and for
pseudomeningoceles to form.
A pseudomeningocele observed on a CT myelogram strongly suggests a nerve root avulsion
(Figure 9).
Figure 9 CT myelograms of the spine of a patient with cervical pseudomeningocele. A, Axial CT
myelogram shows two right-sided cervical pseudomeningoceles (asterisks). B, Axial CT
myelogram shows one right-sided cervical pseudomeningocele (asterisk). The left side shown in
both myelograms is normal. (Reproduced with permission from the Mayo Foundation for Medical
Education and Research, Rochester, MN.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI also may be helpful in evaluating patients in whom nerve root avulsion is suspected.
Advantages of MRI over CT myelography

MRI is noninvasive and can visualize much of the brachial plexus; therefore, it may surpass
CT myelography in the near future.
CT myelography demonstrates only nerve root injury–type BPIs
MRI can reveal large neuromas after trauma and associated inflammation or edema.
In acute trauma, CT myelography remains the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for
nerve root avulsion; however, MRI techniques and sequences continue to improve and may
eliminate the need for myelography in the near future.
Ultrasonography
Recently, ultrasonography has gained popularity.
A recent review demonstrated an overall sensitivity of 87%, with higher accuracy for C5
through C7 roots for detecting injuries.
It is user dependent and often difficult to visualize some neural anatomy secondary to depth
and scar tissue that develops postinjury.
Other Studies
Arteriography
Arteriography should be performed in patients in whom vascular injury is suspected.
Magnetic resonance angiography may be useful to confirm the patency of previous vascular
repair or reconstruction.
Management
Indications
Many patients with a traumatic BPI, especially if mild and blunt in nature, recover
spontaneously over weeks to months. Surgical treatment is indicated only for patients without
the likelihood of spontaneous or additional recovery.
Current surgical management focuses on the restoration of motor function and protective
sensation. Surgical management for restoration of motor function does not address the severe
neuropathic pain associated with avulsion injuries.
Direct nerve repair is preferable in patients with a postganglionic BPI if repair can be
performed without creating excess tension on the affected nerve. This rarely is possible and

occurs only with acute sharp lacerations.
Nerve grafting (the interposition of a donor nerve between the proximal and distal ends of an
injured nerve if the proximal end is viable) should be considered in patients with
postganglionic lesions not amenable to direct repair (Figure 10).
Figure 10 Illustration shows intraplexal nerve grafting, which is used, if possible, for anatomic
brachial plexus reconstruction, including C5 to shoulder targets (suprascapular nerve [A] and
posterior division of the upper trunk [B]), C6 to elbow flexors (anterior division of the upper
trunk [C]), and C7 to extensor muscles (posterior division of the middle trunk [D]). (Reproduced
with permission from the Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Rochester,
MN.)
Nerve grafting is preferable for lesions of the upper and middle trunk because reinnervation of
the proximal shoulder musculature may occur before irreversible changes occur at the motor
end plate.
Nerve grafting of lower trunk lesions often is associated with poor results secondary to the
time to reinnervation of the very distal arm and hand muscles.
Sources of nerve graft include the sural nerve, ipsilateral cutaneous nerves, and ipsilateral
vascularized ulnar nerve (only in patients with a C8/T1 avulsion). These donor nerves typically
are smaller in diameter than the recipient plexus nerves; therefore, they are doubled or
tripled to form a cable nerve graft to match the injured nerve diameter (Figure 11).

Nerve transfers
Nerve transfer refers to the connection of a working but less important motor nerve directly
into the affected, nonfunctional motor nerve of interest to reinnervate a desired muscle.
The two main categories of sources for neurotization are extraplexal and intraplexal.
Extraplexal sources include the spinal accessory nerve (Figure 12, A), intercostal nerves
(Figure 12, B), contralateral C7 nerve, and hypoglossal nerve. The more commonly used
extraplexal nerve transfers in brachial plexus reconstruction involve the use of the spinal
accessory nerve and the intercostal nerves (sensory and motor).
Intraplexal sources include the phrenic nerve, portions of working ulnar or median nerves,
and intact pectoral nerves.

In patients with an upper trunk–type injury, two fascicles of the ulnar nerve can be used as a
source for motor nerve to transfer to the biceps motor branch (Oberlin transfer; Figure 13).
If the median nerve is uninjured, fascicles of the median nerve also can be transferred to the
brachialis motor branch. This is known as a double fascicular transfer for elbow flexion.

A triceps branch of the radial nerve can be transferred to the axillary nerve in patients with

Various combinations of neurotization are used to restore limited function to a patient with a
BPI. The greater the degree of injury, the more limited the results (ie, complete BPIs have
fewer options than upper trunk injuries).

Free-functioning muscle transfer (FFMT) refers to the translocation of a healthy muscle and its
neurovascular pedicle from another part of the body (eg, free gracilis muscle transfer to the
clavicle and proximal forearm).
FFMTs are options to restore elbow flexion in patients with a very late presentation (>1 year)
and an intact vascular status.
The gracilis is the most commonly used muscle for FFMT (Figure 15).
Free-functioning muscles also can be used in the acute setting to obtain grasp, prehension,
and elbow flexion/extension in patients with a complete acute BPI; a double FFMT performed
in two stages may yield this result.
Tendon transfers (such as the trapezius) also may improve upper extremity function greatly in
patients with late presentation or partial paralysis.

Management Based on Type of Injury
Upper trunk injury (C5, C6): avulsion of the C5 and C6 roots; patients present with a flail
shoulder and loss of elbow flexion.
If the avulsion is managed before 6 months, shoulder stability, abduction, and limited
external rotation, as well as elbow flexion can be restored via transfer of the spinal accessory
nerve to the suprascapular nerve, a triceps branch transfer of the radial nerve to the axillary
nerve, and an ulnar nerve fascicle transfer to the biceps motor branch.
Trapezius tendon transfers can improve shoulder external rotation.

Viable surgical treatment options exist to restore shoulder function; therefore, shoulder
arthrodesis is not recommended for the initial management of BPIs.
Studies have reported that after these transfers, 65% to 72% of patients have grade M3 or
greater elbow flexion, and 80% of patients have M3 or greater shoulder abduction4.
Lower trunk injury (C8, T1)
Restoration of hand function has been much less successful than restoration of shoulder and
elbow function.
If avulsions or ruptures involve C8 and T1, tendon transfers are recommended because the
time to reinnervation of the intrinsic muscles exceeds the longevity of the motor end plate.
Transfer of the brachioradialis to the flexor pollicis longus, the extensor carpi radialis or
brachialis to the flexor digitorum profundus, and the extensor indicis proprius for opposition
will restore finger flexion, thumb flexion, and opposition, respectively.
Pan-plexus nerve root avulsions
These traumatic BPIs are associated with the worst prognosis.
Multiple surgical treatment plans are used to manage these injuries; they include all nerve
transfers or a combination of nerve transfers and gracilis FFMTs.
Single or double FFMTs are beyond the scope of this lesson but currently are the optimal
method for restoring varied degrees of grasp, elbow flexion/extension, and shoulder
function.
Combination of nerve transfers and tendon transfers about the shoulder can restore
function in these injuries
Contraindications
The major absolute contraindications to brachial plexus reconstruction are a patient’s
unwillingness to undergo surgical treatment or unrealistic goals.
Relative contraindications are severe elbow or shoulder contracture, advanced age, medical
comorbidities, and traumatic brain injury or cervical spinal cord injury.
Isolated C8-T1 BPIs also are a relative contraindication to brachial plexus reconstruction
because more predictable results may be achieved via distal nerve and/or tendon transfers.

The priorities of the management of BPIs are elbow flexion, shoulder stability (with
abduction and external rotation), hand sensibility, wrist extension/finger flexion, wrist
flexion/finger extension, and intrinsic function. Persistent shoulder instability and lack of
mobility are common and debilitating problems in adult patients with BPI. The lack of
shoulder mobility considerably hinders use of the upper extremity, even if the elbow,
wrist, and fingers are functioning normally. Recovery of deltoid and rotator cuff function
often is incomplete, regardless whether brachial plexus reconstruction has been
performed; such incomplete recovery results in poor abduction and limited or no
external rotation.
For patients who have an upper plexus injury without clinical or electromyographic
evidence of recovery 3 to 6 months postinjury, good functional outcomes for restoration
of elbow flexion and shoulder abduction are achieved via nerve transfers.4 These include
spinal accessory to suprascapular nerve and transfer of part of the radial nerve to the
motor branch of the axillary nerve (Leechavengvongs transfer) for shoulder function.
Oberlin transfer (transfer of part of the ulnar nerve to the motor branch to the biceps) or
double fascicular transfer (Oberlin plus part of medial nerve to motor branch of
brachialis) have been successful for elbow flexion.4 Despite the encouraging results
observed in improvement of shoulder abduction with the nerve transfers, recovery of
external rotation of the shoulder continues to lag behind.4 With limited or absent
shoulder external rotation, most patients maintain an internal rotation position of the
shoulder, which results in a hand-on-belly position. In these instances, patients cannot
position the hand in front of the body in the coronal plane, resulting in substantial
limitation of functional use of the limb. Tendon transfer options to improve external
rotation include the following:
Lower Trapezius Transfer
This transfer can attain considerable improvement in shoulder external rotation with
marginal improvements of shoulder abduction and flexion.5,6
Contralateral Lower Trapezius Transfer
In the absence of available muscles on the ipsilateral side of the injury to transfer to the
infraspinatus to restore shoulder external rotation, contralateral trapezius transfer is a
unique, and may be the only, option. The contralateral lower trapezius muscle origin is

Latissimus Dorsi Transfer
Latissimus dorsi tendon transfer, with or without teres major transfer, is commonly
performed in patients with residual brachial plexus birth palsy to restore abduction and
external rotation.9 Most pediatric plexus injuries involve C5 and C6. In patients with such
injuries, some latissimus function is preserved. In addition, partial recovery of deltoid
and subscapularis function usually is present and is critical for transfer of the latissimus
dorsi to be effective. In patients without deltoid and subscapularis function, latissimus
transfer to the greater tuberosity may magnify the inferior subluxation and adduction-
extension of the shoulder.
In patients with a pan-plexus injury, extraplexal nerve transfers from the spinal
accessory or intercostal nerves are commonly performed to regain some elbow flexion
and shoulder abduction. Often, nerve transfer options are limited in these patients and
alternative reconstructive options are necessary. The trapezius, levator scapulae, and
rhomboids have been reported to be preserved or recovered in 96% of patients with a
plexus injury. The trapezius innervation is extraplexal, and the dorsal scapular nerve
supplying the rhomboids and levator scapulae receives contributions from more

with incomplete plexus palsy, which greatly expands the opportunity for reconstruction.
In patients with a pan-plexus injury in whom limited options are available for nerve
transfers or in patients with an upper plexus injury in whom nerve transfers cannot
restore adequate shoulder abduction, flexion, and external rotation, various tendon
transfer options are available to improve shoulder stability and function.
Upper Trapezius Transfer
This transfer is commonly performed to improve shoulder stabilization and abduction in
patients with a BPI, including those who have previously undergone spinal accessory
nerve transfer as part of brachial plexus reconstruction. Good results in terms of
shoulder stabilization have been reported in the literature.11 Recovery of shoulder
abduction and flexion is better in patients with other functioning muscles about the
shoulder, such as biceps, coracobrachialis, triceps, and pectoralis major, and only
modest improvement in abduction-flexion is observed in patients with complete plexus
injuries.12
Pectoralis Muscle Transfer
Function and preservation of the pectoral nerves are prerequisites in considering and
undertaking this transfer. During transfer of the pectoralis major muscle, the upper
portions (clavicular and upper sternocostal parts) are harvested on their pedicle, and the
muscle is then turned over 180°, with the deep surface being superficial. The muscular
portion is attached to the lateral aspect of the clavicle and the acromion, whereas the
tendinous portion is anchored to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. In isolation, this
technique restores a mean of 40° of abduction. Improved abduction and forward flexion
have been reported with the addition of upper trapezius transfer.13,14
Combined Transfers
A combination of the already mentioned transfers is used to reconstruct shoulder
function. In patients with persistent shoulder instability despite the transfers already
described , glenohumeral arthrodesis may be indicated. In some centers, arthrodesis of
the glenohumeral joint is routinely performed to use the available nerve resources for
elbow flexion-extension and prehension. Nonunion and fracture of the humerus may be
problematic complications after arthrodesis. Contraindications to shoulder arthrodesis
include extensive paralysis of the trapezius and shoulder stabilizers (levator scapulae,
serratus anterior, or rhomboid muscles); if these scapular stabilizing muscles are

force to aid in union. The optimal position for arthrodesis of the shoulder is a subject of
debate. Patients with total paralysis of the brachial plexus and normal function of the
trapezius and serratus anterior muscles should undergo arthrodesis in 30° to 40° of
abduction and flexion and 30° of internal rotation. Conversely, in patients who have total
paralysis of the brachial plexus with absence of serratus anterior or trapezius function,
shoulder arthrodesis should be avoided and performed only if inferior shoulder
subluxation is associated with extensive symptoms. In this situation, the position of
arthrodesis should be 20° of abduction, 10° of flexion, and 30° of internal rotation.

Lower Trapezius Transfer
An incision is made medial to the scapula through which the lower trapezius is harvested
(Figure 17, A and B). The muscle is lengthened (with an Achilles or posterior tibialis
tendon allograft or a hamstring autograft), passed under the deltoid and infraspinatus,
and anchored to the infraspinatus insertion site (Figure 17, C and D). Because almost all
patients with a BPI have an intact infraspinatus tendon insertion, a mean 5 to 7 cm in
length of the infraspinatus tendon can be attained with additional dissection (Figure 18).
This has allowed for modification of the previously mentioned technique by performing
direct transfer of the lower trapezius tendon to the infraspinatus tendon without tendon
allograft augmentation (Figure 19).

Glenohumeral Arthrodesis
The patient is positioned in the beach-chair position. A posterior incision that follows the
spine of the scapula is made and extends down the lateral humeral head and shaft. The

posterior half of the deltoid is detached from the scapular spine and acromion and is
retracted distally. All soft tissue under the acromion is removed, and the rotator cuff
muscles are detached from the greater and lesser tuberosities to expose the joint
capsule, glenohumeral joint, and acromiohumeral joint. Articular cartilage from each
joint is removed to facilitate contact of the subchondral bone of the humeral head and
glenoid cavity. Bone graft from the iliac crest is then inserted into the subacromial space.
The glenohumeral and acromiohumeral joints are transfixed with the use of long
cannulated screws measuring 7.3 mm in diameter in the position of 30° of abduction-
flexion and internal rotation. Because most patients with a BPI have osteopenic bones,
adequate compression of the acromion on the superior surface of the humerus is
important. This allows for additional contact surface, which may maximize the fusion
rate. A 4.5-mm pelvic reconstruction plate is contoured to the scapular spine and
humerus and is secured in place, which adds substantial stiffness to the fusion
construct. Cancellous bone chips are used to pack the vacant space of both joints
(Figure 21).

Preoperative Evaluation
Good strength of the trapezius and rhomboid
No contracture of the scapulothoracic joint
Pearls
Provides stability to the shoulder
Improvement in range of shoulder motion, depending on the strength of the
scapulothoracic muscles
Pitfalls
Postoperative fracture of the humerus
Risk of nonunion
Impairment of turning during sleep
Postoperative Management
Splint or shoulder immobilizer for 3 months
Gentle range of motion exercises of the scapulothoracic joint
Radiographs monthly until healing
The goal of shoulder arthrodesis after BPI is to stabilize the glenohumeral joint and
permit the patient to move the upper part of the arm through the scapulothoracic joint
with the use of innervated scapular muscles. Postoperative range of shoulder movement
depends on the residual strength of the periscapular muscles, such as the trapezius,
levator scapulae, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi, and rhomboid muscles.
